title: Zeroness of rational weighted context-free grammars
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that always halts and decides whether \(f_G(w)=0\) for every finite word \(w\in\Sigma^{*}\), given a context-free grammar in the weighted normal form below with rational production weights? Here \(f_G(w)\) is the sum, over all parse trees with yield \(w\), of the product of their production weights. Rational weights may be negative. This card selects the rational weighted-grammar case of the source’s broader zeroness agenda.
why: This is an identity test for recursive numerical descriptions, extending finite-state weighted equivalence to context-free composition. It isolates the difficulty of exact cancellation across arbitrarily deep but finitely parsed derivations, a basic obstacle behind comparing quantitative grammars and counting their parses.
status_note: The 2021 seminar direction and 2024 primary paper identify weighted context-free zeroness as unresolved. The 2023 results concern commutative series or restricted word languages. A bounded search on 13 September 2026 found no decision theorem for the selected rational finite-parse grammar model; this is not exhaustive current-openness certification.

sentences: A weighted context-free grammar assigns each word the sum of the weights of its parse trees.
This card asks whether an algorithm can always decide if that value is zero for every finite word.
Production weights are signed rationals, and an explicit normal form ensures every word has only finitely many parses.
The challenge is cancellation for each ordered word; results on commuting-variable series and weighted parallel processes address different models.
The rational grammar variant is an explicit editorial choice from a broader source agenda, with decidability or undecidability to be proved in Lean.

definitions: The input has finite disjoint sets of nonterminals \(V\) and terminals \(\Sigma\), with \(\Sigma\ne\varnothing\), a start nonterminal \(S\in V\), and finitely many productions. Every production has one of the forms \(A\to BC\) or \(A\to a\), with \(A,B,C\in V\) and \(a\in\Sigma\); additionally \(S\to\varepsilon\) is allowed. The start symbol never occurs on a right-hand side. Each production has a rational weight, explicitly encoded by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. At most one production with each left- and right-hand side is listed. There are no unit productions or other empty productions. Zero weights are allowed.

A parse tree is a finite ordered tree rooted at \(S\). Each nonterminal node expands by a listed production; the terminal leaves in order give its yield, and the empty start production gives the empty yield. The weight of a tree is the product of all weights of the productions used at its nonterminal nodes. The same production used at several nodes contributes one factor for every occurrence.

For a nonempty word of length \(m\), a parse tree in this form has \(m\) terminal-producing nodes and \(m-1\) binary-producing nodes. Thus there are only finitely many parses for each word, even when the grammar is ambiguous. Their rational weights are summed to define \(f_G(w)\); an empty sum is zero. For the empty word the value is the weight of \(S\to\varepsilon\), or zero if that production is absent. No analytic convergence or infinite sums of derivations are involved.

Terminal order is preserved: words with the same numbers of letters can have different values. Zeroness concerns the full function on words, not its commutative generating function or sums over word lengths. Cancellation between positive and negative tree weights is part of the semantics; there is no nonnegativity or probabilistic normalization promise.

All symbols and productions are listed explicitly with delimited binary indices. The algorithm is one ordinary deterministic Turing machine on finite descriptions, halting on every well-formed input and returning yes exactly for identically zero functions. No time bound is imposed; malformed descriptions can be rejected. The explicit binary normal form and coefficient field \(\mathbb{Q}\) are editorial choices fixing one benchmark variant.
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating decision algorithm for this rational weighted-grammar zeroness problem, or a Lean-checked undecidability proof. Testing finitely many sampled words, deciding zero only on a unary or bounded language, or deciding a commutative generating-series identity does not settle the stated word-by-word problem.

context_blocks.text: The seminar’s question lists several separate models: weighted grammars over a field, unary polynomial automata, weighted Parikh automata and weighted vector addition systems. This benchmark retains the grammar branch with rational coefficients and an explicit finite-parse normal form. It does not claim that solving this selected variant settles the other listed models.

Clemente’s 2024 paper still identifies rational weighted context-free grammar zeroness as beyond known techniques. It obtains decidability for weighted basic parallel processes, whose interleaving composition is different from sequential grammar concatenation.

The 2023 algebraic-series results concern commuting variables and multiplicity comparisons on restricted languages. Those results do not determine cancellation separately for every ordered word in an unrestricted alphabet.

statement_review.notes: Selected rational weighted context-free grammar zeroness from the source’s four-model agenda, explicitly labeling the coefficient field and binary normal form as editorial choices. Defined finite ordered parse semantics, signed products and sums, the empty word, syntactic encoding and total decidability. Avoided infinite derivation sums and kept noncommutative word identities distinct from solved commutative and parallel-process problems.
